## Buy a House After Bankruptcy in District of Columbia [2026]: Waiting Periods + DC DPA
Source: https://buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com/states/district-of-columbia.html

← buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com home

Buy a House After Bankruptcy in District of Columbia [2026]: Waiting Periods + DC DPA

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for District of Columbia residents.

Buying a Home After Bankruptcy in District of Columbia - Federal Waiting Periods

Waiting periods are federal and apply uniformly in District of Columbia. The state-specific layer is down-payment assistance and homestead protection, not the underlying loan program.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

VA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

USDA3 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Conventional (Fannie/Freddie)4 years from discharge (2 years with extenuating circumstances)2 years from discharge or 4 years from dismissal

Jumbo (non-conforming)7 years typical7 years typical

"Extenuating circumstances" (job loss, medical event, divorce) can reduce waiting periods. See FHA guide and conventional mortgage guide.

District of Columbia Down-Payment Assistance Programs

DC Open Doors and HPAP (Home Purchase Assistance Program) - up to $202,000 in DPA for DC residents.

These state-level programs are compatible with post-bankruptcy borrowers who meet the federal waiting period. Key considerations for District of Columbia DPA:

First-time buyer requirement. "First time" is usually defined as no home ownership in the past 3 years. A prior bankruptcy does not restart this clock; selling the home pre-petition can.

Income limits. Most District of Columbia DPA is capped by household income (typically 80-140% of area median income).

Credit minimums. District of Columbia DPA generally requires 620-640 minimum credit score; rebuilding after bankruptcy is the path.

Purchase price caps. District of Columbia DPA programs cap purchase prices by county.

Homebuyer education. Most District of Columbia DPA requires 8-hour HUD-approved homebuyer education class (separate from bankruptcy credit counseling).

Owner-occupancy. Must be primary residence, not investment or second home.

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in District of Columbia

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy District of Columbia homebuyers. A typical District of Columbia rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for District of Columbia DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

District of Columbia Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

District of Columbia homestead exemption: Unlimited (DC Code 15-501).

The District of Columbia homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the District of Columbia homestead exemption is generous (District of Columbia is very generous - unlimited), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the District of Columbia homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. District of Columbia judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See District of Columbia full exemption list.

Loan Officer Conversations After District of Columbia Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a District of Columbia lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

District of Columbia Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In District of Columbia, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

District of Columbia Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural District of Columbia; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Related District of Columbia Resources

FHA loan detail

Conventional mortgage detail

Down-payment assistance

Credit rebuild

District of Columbia exemptions

See Idaho full exemption list.

Loan Officer Conversations After Idaho Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a Idaho lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

Idaho Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In Idaho, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Idaho Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Idaho; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

## Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Illinois [2026]: Waiting Periods + IL DPA
Source: https://buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com/states/illinois.html

← buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com home

Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Illinois [2026]: Waiting Periods + IL DPA

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Illinois residents.

Buying a Home After Bankruptcy in Illinois - Federal Waiting Periods

Waiting periods are federal and apply uniformly in Illinois. The state-specific layer is down-payment assistance and homestead protection, not the underlying loan program.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

VA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

USDA3 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Conventional (Fannie/Freddie)4 years from discharge (2 years with extenuating circumstances)2 years from discharge or 4 years from dismissal

Jumbo (non-conforming)7 years typical7 years typical

"Extenuating circumstances" (job loss, medical event, divorce) can reduce waiting periods. See FHA guide and conventional mortgage guide.

Illinois Down-Payment Assistance Programs

IHDA (Illinois Housing Development Authority) Access programs - forgivable DPA up to 10% of purchase price.

These state-level programs are compatible with post-bankruptcy borrowers who meet the federal waiting period. Key considerations for Illinois DPA:

First-time buyer requirement. "First time" is usually defined as no home ownership in the past 3 years. A prior bankruptcy does not restart this clock; selling the home pre-petition can.

Income limits. Most Illinois DPA is capped by household income (typically 80-140% of area median income).

Credit minimums. Illinois DPA generally requires 620-640 minimum credit score; rebuilding after bankruptcy is the path.

Purchase price caps. Illinois DPA programs cap purchase prices by county.

Homebuyer education. Most Illinois DPA requires 8-hour HUD-approved homebuyer education class (separate from bankruptcy credit counseling).

Owner-occupancy. Must be primary residence, not investment or second home.

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in Illinois

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy Illinois homebuyers. A typical Illinois rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for Illinois DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

Illinois Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

Illinois homestead exemption: $15,000 (735 ILCS 5/12-901).

The Illinois homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the Illinois homestead exemption is generous (Illinois is capped at $15,000), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the Illinois homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. Illinois judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See Illinois full exemption list.

Illinois Federal Bankruptcy Data

Many Illinois homebuyers arriving at the mortgage-qualification conversation have a prior bankruptcy discharge. These FJC numbers show Illinois's bankruptcy resolution context.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 9,898 consumer bankruptcy cases from Illinois's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 76,72999.5%0.4%

Chapter 133,16945.9%53.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

Illinois Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In Illinois, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Illinois Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Illinois; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Related Kansas Resources

## Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Kentucky [2026]: Waiting Periods + KY DPA
Source: https://buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com/states/kentucky.html

← buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com home

Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Kentucky [2026]: Waiting Periods + KY DPA

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Kentucky residents.

Buying a Home After Bankruptcy in Kentucky - Federal Waiting Periods

Waiting periods are federal and apply uniformly in Kentucky. The state-specific layer is down-payment assistance and homestead protection, not the underlying loan program.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

VA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

USDA3 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Conventional (Fannie/Freddie)4 years from discharge (2 years with extenuating circumstances)2 years from discharge or 4 years from dismissal

Jumbo (non-conforming)7 years typical7 years typical

"Extenuating circumstances" (job loss, medical event, divorce) can reduce waiting periods. See FHA guide and conventional mortgage guide.

Kentucky Down-Payment Assistance Programs

Kentucky Housing Corp Regular DAP ($10,000 at 1% amortized over 10 years).

These state-level programs are compatible with post-bankruptcy borrowers who meet the federal waiting period. Key considerations for Kentucky DPA:

First-time buyer requirement. "First time" is usually defined as no home ownership in the past 3 years. A prior bankruptcy does not restart this clock; selling the home pre-petition can.

Income limits. Most Kentucky DPA is capped by household income (typically 80-140% of area median income).

Credit minimums. Kentucky DPA generally requires 620-640 minimum credit score; rebuilding after bankruptcy is the path.

Purchase price caps. Kentucky DPA programs cap purchase prices by county.

Homebuyer education. Most Kentucky DPA requires 8-hour HUD-approved homebuyer education class (separate from bankruptcy credit counseling).

Owner-occupancy. Must be primary residence, not investment or second home.

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in Kentucky

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy Kentucky homebuyers. A typical Kentucky rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for Kentucky DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

Kentucky Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

Kentucky homestead exemption: $5,000 (KRS 427.060).

The Kentucky homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the Kentucky homestead exemption is generous (Kentucky is capped at $5,000), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the Kentucky homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. Kentucky judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See Kentucky full exemption list.

Kentucky Federal Bankruptcy Data

Many Kentucky homebuyers arriving at the mortgage-qualification conversation have a prior bankruptcy discharge. These FJC numbers show Kentucky's bankruptcy resolution context.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,692 consumer bankruptcy cases from Kentucky's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 731897.5%1.7%

Chapter 131,37472.1%27.0%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Loan Officer Conversations After Kentucky Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a Kentucky lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

Kentucky Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In Kentucky, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Kentucky Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Kentucky; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Related Kentucky Resources

Conventional mortgage detail

Massachusetts Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

Massachusetts homestead exemption: $500,000 (automatic) / $1M declared (M.G.L. c.188).

The Massachusetts homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the Massachusetts homestead exemption is generous (Massachusetts is capped at $500,000), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the Massachusetts homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. Massachusetts judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See Massachusetts full exemption list.

Massachusetts Federal Bankruptcy Data

Many Massachusetts homebuyers arriving at the mortgage-qualification conversation have a prior bankruptcy discharge. These FJC numbers show Massachusetts's bankruptcy resolution context.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,356 consumer bankruptcy cases from Massachusetts's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 71,29098.3%0.9%

Chapter 136659.1%40.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Loan Officer Conversations After Massachusetts Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a Massachusetts lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

Massachusetts Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In Massachusetts, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Massachusetts Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Massachusetts; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

## Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Michigan [2026]: Waiting Periods + MI DPA
Source: https://buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com/states/michigan.html

← buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com home

Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Michigan [2026]: Waiting Periods + MI DPA

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Michigan residents.

Buying a Home After Bankruptcy in Michigan - Federal Waiting Periods

Waiting periods are federal and apply uniformly in Michigan. The state-specific layer is down-payment assistance and homestead protection, not the underlying loan program.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

VA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

USDA3 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Conventional (Fannie/Freddie)4 years from discharge (2 years with extenuating circumstances)2 years from discharge or 4 years from dismissal

Jumbo (non-conforming)7 years typical7 years typical

"Extenuating circumstances" (job loss, medical event, divorce) can reduce waiting periods. See FHA guide and conventional mortgage guide.

Michigan Down-Payment Assistance Programs

MSHDA (Michigan State Housing Development Authority) MI Home Loan + DPA up to $10,000.

These state-level programs are compatible with post-bankruptcy borrowers who meet the federal waiting period. Key considerations for Michigan DPA:

First-time buyer requirement. "First time" is usually defined as no home ownership in the past 3 years. A prior bankruptcy does not restart this clock; selling the home pre-petition can.

Income limits. Most Michigan DPA is capped by household income (typically 80-140% of area median income).

Credit minimums. Michigan DPA generally requires 620-640 minimum credit score; rebuilding after bankruptcy is the path.

Purchase price caps. Michigan DPA programs cap purchase prices by county.

Homebuyer education. Most Michigan DPA requires 8-hour HUD-approved homebuyer education class (separate from bankruptcy credit counseling).

Owner-occupancy. Must be primary residence, not investment or second home.

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in Michigan

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy Michigan homebuyers. A typical Michigan rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for Michigan DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

Michigan Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

Michigan homestead exemption: $46,125 ($69,200 if 65+/disabled) (MCL 600.5451).

The Michigan homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the Michigan homestead exemption is generous (Michigan is capped at $46,125), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the Michigan homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. Michigan judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See Michigan full exemption list.

Michigan Federal Bankruptcy Data

Many Michigan homebuyers arriving at the mortgage-qualification conversation have a prior bankruptcy discharge. These FJC numbers show Michigan's bankruptcy resolution context.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,133 consumer bankruptcy cases from Michigan's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7633100.0%0.0%

Chapter 1350048.3%51.0%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Michigan Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In Michigan, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Michigan Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Michigan; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Related Missouri Resources

## Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Montana [2026]: Waiting Periods + MT DPA
Source: https://buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com/states/montana.html

← buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com home

Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Montana [2026]: Waiting Periods + MT DPA

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Montana residents.

Buying a Home After Bankruptcy in Montana - Federal Waiting Periods

Waiting periods are federal and apply uniformly in Montana. The state-specific layer is down-payment assistance and homestead protection, not the underlying loan program.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

VA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

USDA3 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Conventional (Fannie/Freddie)4 years from discharge (2 years with extenuating circumstances)2 years from discharge or 4 years from dismissal

Jumbo (non-conforming)7 years typical7 years typical

"Extenuating circumstances" (job loss, medical event, divorce) can reduce waiting periods. See FHA guide and conventional mortgage guide.

Montana Down-Payment Assistance Programs

Montana Housing Regular Bond with Bond Advantage DPA ($15,000 0% amortized).

These state-level programs are compatible with post-bankruptcy borrowers who meet the federal waiting period. Key considerations for Montana DPA:

First-time buyer requirement. "First time" is usually defined as no home ownership in the past 3 years. A prior bankruptcy does not restart this clock; selling the home pre-petition can.

Income limits. Most Montana DPA is capped by household income (typically 80-140% of area median income).

Credit minimums. Montana DPA generally requires 620-640 minimum credit score; rebuilding after bankruptcy is the path.

Purchase price caps. Montana DPA programs cap purchase prices by county.

Homebuyer education. Most Montana DPA requires 8-hour HUD-approved homebuyer education class (separate from bankruptcy credit counseling).

Owner-occupancy. Must be primary residence, not investment or second home.

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in Montana

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy Montana homebuyers. A typical Montana rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for Montana DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

Montana Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

Montana homestead exemption: $378,560 (MCA 70-32-104).

The Montana homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the Montana homestead exemption is generous (Montana is capped at $378,560), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the Montana homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. Montana judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See Montana full exemption list.

Loan Officer Conversations After Montana Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a Montana lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

Montana Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In Montana, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Montana Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Montana; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Related Montana Resources

Conventional mortgage detail

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

New Jersey Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

New Jersey homestead exemption: $0 (federal opt-in common) (federal $31,575/2025).

The New Jersey homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the New Jersey homestead exemption is generous (New Jersey is capped at $0), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the New Jersey homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. New Jersey judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See New Jersey full exemption list.

New Jersey Federal Bankruptcy Data

Many New Jersey homebuyers arriving at the mortgage-qualification conversation have a prior bankruptcy discharge. These FJC numbers show New Jersey's bankruptcy resolution context.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,580 consumer bankruptcy cases from New Jersey's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 752697.3%2.7%

Chapter 131,05431.0%68.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Loan Officer Conversations After New Jersey Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a New Jersey lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

New Jersey Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In New Jersey, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

New Jersey Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural New Jersey; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

## Buy a House After Bankruptcy in New Mexico [2026]: Waiting Periods + NM DPA
Source: https://buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com/states/new-mexico.html

← buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com home

Buy a House After Bankruptcy in New Mexico [2026]: Waiting Periods + NM DPA

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Mexico residents.

Buying a Home After Bankruptcy in New Mexico - Federal Waiting Periods

Waiting periods are federal and apply uniformly in New Mexico. The state-specific layer is down-payment assistance and homestead protection, not the underlying loan program.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

VA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

USDA3 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Conventional (Fannie/Freddie)4 years from discharge (2 years with extenuating circumstances)2 years from discharge or 4 years from dismissal

Jumbo (non-conforming)7 years typical7 years typical

"Extenuating circumstances" (job loss, medical event, divorce) can reduce waiting periods. See FHA guide and conventional mortgage guide.

New Mexico Down-Payment Assistance Programs

MFA (NM Mortgage Finance Authority) FirstDown ($8,000 DPA, 10-year forgivable).

These state-level programs are compatible with post-bankruptcy borrowers who meet the federal waiting period. Key considerations for New Mexico DPA:

First-time buyer requirement. "First time" is usually defined as no home ownership in the past 3 years. A prior bankruptcy does not restart this clock; selling the home pre-petition can.

Income limits. Most New Mexico DPA is capped by household income (typically 80-140% of area median income).

Credit minimums. New Mexico DPA generally requires 620-640 minimum credit score; rebuilding after bankruptcy is the path.

Purchase price caps. New Mexico DPA programs cap purchase prices by county.

Homebuyer education. Most New Mexico DPA requires 8-hour HUD-approved homebuyer education class (separate from bankruptcy credit counseling).

Owner-occupancy. Must be primary residence, not investment or second home.

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in New Mexico

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy New Mexico homebuyers. A typical New Mexico rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for New Mexico DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

New Mexico Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

New Mexico homestead exemption: $150,000 (NMSA 42-10-9).

The New Mexico homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the New Mexico homestead exemption is generous (New Mexico is capped at $150,000), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the New Mexico homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. New Mexico judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See New Mexico full exemption list.

Loan Officer Conversations After New Mexico Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a New Mexico lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

New Mexico Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In New Mexico, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

New Mexico Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural New Mexico; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural North Dakota; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Related North Dakota Resources

Conventional mortgage detail

## Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Ohio [2026]: Waiting Periods + OH DPA
Source: https://buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com/states/ohio.html

← buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com home

Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Ohio [2026]: Waiting Periods + OH DPA

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Buying a Home After Bankruptcy in Ohio - Federal Waiting Periods

Waiting periods are federal and apply uniformly in Ohio. The state-specific layer is down-payment assistance and homestead protection, not the underlying loan program.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

VA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

USDA3 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Conventional (Fannie/Freddie)4 years from discharge (2 years with extenuating circumstances)2 years from discharge or 4 years from dismissal

Jumbo (non-conforming)7 years typical7 years typical

"Extenuating circumstances" (job loss, medical event, divorce) can reduce waiting periods. See FHA guide and conventional mortgage guide.

Ohio Down-Payment Assistance Programs

Ohio Housing Finance Agency (OHFA) YourChoice! DPA up to 5% of purchase price.

These state-level programs are compatible with post-bankruptcy borrowers who meet the federal waiting period. Key considerations for Ohio DPA:

First-time buyer requirement. "First time" is usually defined as no home ownership in the past 3 years. A prior bankruptcy does not restart this clock; selling the home pre-petition can.

Income limits. Most Ohio DPA is capped by household income (typically 80-140% of area median income).

Credit minimums. Ohio DPA generally requires 620-640 minimum credit score; rebuilding after bankruptcy is the path.

Purchase price caps. Ohio DPA programs cap purchase prices by county.

Homebuyer education. Most Ohio DPA requires 8-hour HUD-approved homebuyer education class (separate from bankruptcy credit counseling).

Owner-occupancy. Must be primary residence, not investment or second home.

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in Ohio

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy Ohio homebuyers. A typical Ohio rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for Ohio DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

Ohio Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

Ohio homestead exemption: $161,375 (ORC 2329.66(A)(1) (indexed)).

The Ohio homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the Ohio homestead exemption is generous (Ohio is capped at $161,375), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the Ohio homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. Ohio judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See Ohio full exemption list.

Ohio Federal Bankruptcy Data

Many Ohio homebuyers arriving at the mortgage-qualification conversation have a prior bankruptcy discharge. These FJC numbers show Ohio's bankruptcy resolution context.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 3,971 consumer bankruptcy cases from Ohio's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 73,53597.7%1.8%

Chapter 1343651.1%48.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Loan Officer Conversations After Ohio Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a Ohio lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

Ohio Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In Ohio, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Ohio Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Ohio; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Conventional mortgage detail

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in Rhode Island

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy Rhode Island homebuyers. A typical Rhode Island rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for Rhode Island DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

Rhode Island Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

Rhode Island homestead exemption: $500,000 (R.I.G.L. 9-26-4.1).

The Rhode Island homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the Rhode Island homestead exemption is generous (Rhode Island is capped at $500,000), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the Rhode Island homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. Rhode Island judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See Rhode Island full exemption list.

Loan Officer Conversations After Rhode Island Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a Rhode Island lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

Rhode Island Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In Rhode Island, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Rhode Island Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Rhode Island; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Related Rhode Island Resources

Conventional mortgage detail

## Buy a House After Bankruptcy in South Carolina [2026]: Waiting Periods + SC DPA
Source: https://buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com/states/south-carolina.html

← buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com home

Buy a House After Bankruptcy in South Carolina [2026]: Waiting Periods + SC DPA

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for South Carolina residents.

Buying a Home After Bankruptcy in South Carolina - Federal Waiting Periods

Waiting periods are federal and apply uniformly in South Carolina. The state-specific layer is down-payment assistance and homestead protection, not the underlying loan program.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

VA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

USDA3 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Conventional (Fannie/Freddie)4 years from discharge (2 years with extenuating circumstances)2 years from discharge or 4 years from dismissal

Jumbo (non-conforming)7 years typical7 years typical

"Extenuating circumstances" (job loss, medical event, divorce) can reduce waiting periods. See FHA guide and conventional mortgage guide.

South Carolina Down-Payment Assistance Programs

SC Housing Homebuyer Program Forgivable DPA ($15,000 over 20 years).

These state-level programs are compatible with post-bankruptcy borrowers who meet the federal waiting period. Key considerations for South Carolina DPA:

First-time buyer requirement. "First time" is usually defined as no home ownership in the past 3 years. A prior bankruptcy does not restart this clock; selling the home pre-petition can.

Income limits. Most South Carolina DPA is capped by household income (typically 80-140% of area median income).

Credit minimums. South Carolina DPA generally requires 620-640 minimum credit score; rebuilding after bankruptcy is the path.

Purchase price caps. South Carolina DPA programs cap purchase prices by county.

Homebuyer education. Most South Carolina DPA requires 8-hour HUD-approved homebuyer education class (separate from bankruptcy credit counseling).

Owner-occupancy. Must be primary residence, not investment or second home.

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in South Carolina

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy South Carolina homebuyers. A typical South Carolina rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for South Carolina DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

South Carolina homestead exemption: $67,100 ($134,200 joint, indexed) (S.C. Code 15-41-30).

The South Carolina homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the South Carolina homestead exemption is generous (South Carolina is capped at $67,100), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the South Carolina homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. South Carolina judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See South Carolina full exemption list.

South Carolina Federal Bankruptcy Data

Many South Carolina homebuyers arriving at the mortgage-qualification conversation have a prior bankruptcy discharge. These FJC numbers show South Carolina's bankruptcy resolution context.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 635 consumer bankruptcy cases from South Carolina's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7301n/an/a

Chapter 13334n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

In South Carolina, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Texas Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Texas; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Related Texas Resources

FHA loan detail

Conventional mortgage detail

Down-payment assistance

Texas exemptions

## Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Utah [2026]: Waiting Periods + UT DPA
Source: https://buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com/states/utah.html

← buyahouseafterbankruptcy.com home

Buy a House After Bankruptcy in Utah [2026]: Waiting Periods + UT DPA

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Utah residents.

Buying a Home After Bankruptcy in Utah - Federal Waiting Periods

Waiting periods are federal and apply uniformly in Utah. The state-specific layer is down-payment assistance and homestead protection, not the underlying loan program.

Loan TypeAfter Chapter 7After Chapter 13

FHA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

VA2 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

USDA3 years from discharge1 year of on-time plan payments + court permission

Conventional (Fannie/Freddie)4 years from discharge (2 years with extenuating circumstances)2 years from discharge or 4 years from dismissal

Jumbo (non-conforming)7 years typical7 years typical

"Extenuating circumstances" (job loss, medical event, divorce) can reduce waiting periods. See FHA guide and conventional mortgage guide.

Utah Down-Payment Assistance Programs

Utah Housing Corp FirstHome + DPA second mortgage (up to 6% of loan amount).

These state-level programs are compatible with post-bankruptcy borrowers who meet the federal waiting period. Key considerations for Utah DPA:

First-time buyer requirement. "First time" is usually defined as no home ownership in the past 3 years. A prior bankruptcy does not restart this clock; selling the home pre-petition can.

Income limits. Most Utah DPA is capped by household income (typically 80-140% of area median income).

Credit minimums. Utah DPA generally requires 620-640 minimum credit score; rebuilding after bankruptcy is the path.

Purchase price caps. Utah DPA programs cap purchase prices by county.

Homebuyer education. Most Utah DPA requires 8-hour HUD-approved homebuyer education class (separate from bankruptcy credit counseling).

Owner-occupancy. Must be primary residence, not investment or second home.

See down-payment assistance overview.

Rebuilding Credit in Utah

Credit-rebuild is the rate-limiting step for most post-bankruptcy Utah homebuyers. A typical Utah rebuild arc:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card ($200-$500 deposit); automatic payment to utilities; begin tracking FICO monthly.

Month 6-12: Second tradeline (credit-builder loan or authorized user); target 580+ FICO.

Month 12-24: Unsecured card graduation; auto loan if needed (rate will be poor, focus on on-time payment history); target 620+ FICO.

Month 24-36: Target 640+ FICO for Utah DPA eligibility; build 3 tradelines with 12+ months of on-time history.

Month 36-48: At 4-year mark (conventional) or earlier (FHA/VA), meet waiting-period and credit minimums simultaneously.

See credit rebuild guide.

Utah Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

Utah homestead exemption: $42,700 (Utah Code 78B-5-503).

The Utah homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the Utah homestead exemption is generous (Utah is capped at $42,700), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the Utah homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. Utah judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See Utah full exemption list.

Loan Officer Conversations After Utah Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a Utah lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

Utah Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In Utah, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

Utah Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural Utah; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.

Related Utah Resources

Conventional mortgage detail

West Virginia Homestead Exemption - Why It Matters Before You Buy

West Virginia homestead exemption: $35,000 (W. Va. Code 38-10-4).

The West Virginia homestead exemption protects equity in your primary residence from most creditors. It is most relevant before you file bankruptcy (to plan equity below the exemption cap) but also matters for post-discharge planning:

Equity headroom. If the West Virginia homestead exemption is generous (West Virginia is capped at $35,000), you have flexibility for home appreciation without equity-stripping risk.

Future financial shocks. If you face another financial crisis post-discharge, the West Virginia homestead protects equity up to the exemption amount.

Judgment liens. West Virginia judgment creditors may file liens against your post-discharge home for non-dischargeable debts (DSO, fraud, some taxes).

See West Virginia full exemption list.

West Virginia Federal Bankruptcy Data

Many West Virginia homebuyers arriving at the mortgage-qualification conversation have a prior bankruptcy discharge. These FJC numbers show West Virginia's bankruptcy resolution context.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 60 consumer bankruptcy cases from West Virginia's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 75498.1%1.9%

Chapter 136n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Loan Officer Conversations After West Virginia Bankruptcy

Expect these questions from a West Virginia lender:

Discharge date. Have the official discharge order (it's the starting point for the waiting clock).

Cause of bankruptcy. Lenders look for "non-recurring" explanations (medical, divorce, job loss) versus recurring financial management concerns.

Post-discharge payment history. 12-24 months of on-time rent, utilities, secured credit.

Current debt-to-income (DTI). FHA max is 57% back-end; conventional typically 45-50%.

Reserves. 2-3 months of PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) in savings.

Employment stability. Same employer or industry for 2 years preferred.

Be direct and factual. Do not volunteer context that doesn't help. Do not hide the bankruptcy - lenders will find it in 30 seconds.

West Virginia Chapter 13 Path to Homeownership

Chapter 13 is often overlooked as a path to post-bankruptcy homeownership. The federal rule: after 1 year of on-time Chapter 13 plan payments, FHA and VA allow mortgage qualification during the plan - with court permission.

Complete 12 months on-time. No missed plan payments.

Trustee consent. Request written non-objection from the Chapter 13 trustee.

Court authorization. File motion with the bankruptcy court for approval to incur debt.

Disposable income test. Mortgage payment must fit within (or replace) the housing component of your plan budget.

Lender qualification. You still need to qualify under FHA/VA credit and income standards.

In West Virginia, this is a real pathway. Ask your Chapter 13 trustee whether they have a standard "motion to incur debt" template. See FAQ on in-plan mortgages.

West Virginia Non-Purchase Housing Options Post-Discharge

If waiting-period and credit barriers make purchase infeasible immediately, consider:

Rent to own. Carefully review the contract; many are predatory. Prefer a traditional lease with optional purchase.

Seller financing / land contract. Common in rural West Virginia; offers flexibility but carries risk if seller carries an underlying mortgage with due-on-sale.

Family loan or joint purchase. A family member with strong credit co-signs or holds title; documented intra-family loan for the down payment.

Manufactured home on owned land. Lower price point; FHA Title II applies with 2-year wait post-discharge.

Non-QM loan. Alternative-documentation loans (bank statement, asset-based) available at higher rates for borrowers at 2-3 years post-discharge.
